extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, scientometrics scholars, and research-integrity practitioners interested in retractions and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Profile and analyze scientific article retractions for the top 20 World Class Universities (THE 2020) using Web of Science data (2010–2019), classifying reasons for retraction and measuring journal/university-level metrics. Includes methodology for search, categorization, and statistical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPE retraction guidelines (2020)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions should avoid defamatory language; be published free of charge and immediately in all versions of the journal; ensure that the retraction is clearly identified as such, including the title and authors; and highlight the reason for the article’s withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COPE recommends these practices to minimize harmful effects and further dissemination of the error. Cited as editorial guidance for how retraction notices ought to be issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required transparency in retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions must describe the reason for withdrawal, indicate those responsible for the misconduct (if any), and identify any other factors that resulted in the retraction of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or evasive retraction notices make it difficult to distinguish misconduct from honest error and lead to underestimation of fraudulent articles; clear reporting supports correction of the literature and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction reasons taxonomy (Table 2 / COPE 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize retraction reasons into: Data results (falsification, fabrication, unreliable results); Plagiarism (including self-plagiarism); Redundant publication (same article published more than once); Unethical research (publication without consent of authors, lack of references, image description/editing errors, non-recognition of funding, misuse/disputed data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the study's coding scheme to classify reasons for each retraction; provides operational categories for analysis and counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed misconduct-type categories to code
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific misconduct types to identify include self-plagiarism, data concealment, flawed procedures in data collection, inadequate data retention and storage, incorrect authorship, salami slicing, bias and conflicts of interest, intentional erroneous use of statistical methods, publication of images without permission, inclusion of authors who did not contribute, limited participation in provision of funds/materials/equipment, and fake peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These granular categories supplement the broader taxonomy and help distinguish kinds of misconduct vs honest error during classification and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and inclusion criteria for identifying retractions in WoS
rubrics_metrics.description: Search documents in Web of Science using Boolean OR for terms: 'retracted', 'retraction', 'withdrawal', 'redress'; select document types: retracted publication, retraction, correction; for each target university select the organization affiliation; limit by time window (2010–2019); discard duplicates, not-found records, and those outside the interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions with authors from two or more selected universities were counted once for each university. The search was performed in May 2020. This provides a reproducible sampling procedure for gathering retraction records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction counting and deduplication rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After search, count retractions per university while disregarding duplicate documents, records not found, and those outside the defined time interval; treat multi-affiliated retractions as one retraction for each affiliated university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures consistency in calculating the number of retractions and retraction rates per institution; example: initial 397 reduced to 330 after exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction rate metric (per university)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction rate = (number of retractions indexed in WoS for the institution during period) / (number of articles published by the institution in WoS during period) expressed as a percentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare institutions of different output sizes (example: total publications 1,535,266 and 330 retractions → 0.021% overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variables to collect for each retraction (profiling variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect journal-level and article-level variables: journal impact factor (JCR), language of publication, whether the journal is a COPE member, person responsible for retraction (author/editor/both/not specified), year of publication, year of retraction, time between publication and retraction, and country/institution affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variables enable cross-tabulations (e.g., distribution of retractions by JCR band, language statistics, COPE membership rates) and support interpretation of drivers and patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact factor / JCR band as an analytic dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the distribution of retractions across Journal Citation Report (JCR) impact factor bands (e.g., 3–3.99, 10–19.99) to assess whether retractions concentrate in particular impact ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study finds mixed results; presence of retractions in both high and low impact journals and no simple rule that higher IF equals more retractions. Use JCR (specific years) aligned to retraction data for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-retraction metric and temporal trend analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure time (in years) between article publication and retraction, report averages and distribution; analyze counts of retractions by year of publication and year of retraction to detect temporal trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: average time to retraction 3.20 ± 3.11 years; trend analyses can show whether elapsed time is decreasing and identify peaks in particular years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person responsible for retraction: coding scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Code who is listed as responsible for initiating the retraction: author(s), editor, both author(s) and editor, or unspecified. Recognize 'heroic act' when retraction is requested by the author(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to examine patterns (e.g., authors listed in 43.64% of cases in this study) and to interpret community response and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of prolific retractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify authors with multiple retractions ('prolific retractors') and quantify their contribution to the total number of retractions (e.g., a small number of authors responsible for a large share).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High counts of retractions by a few authors suggest deliberate misconduct rather than isolated honest errors; useful for investigating systemic fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis standards used
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive statistics (mean, frequency, percentage); perform Pearson's correlation coefficient for parametric data with significance threshold p < 0.05 and interpret magnitude as: weak 0.1–0.3, moderate 0.4–0.6, strong 0.7–0.9; use simple linear regression when testing predictive relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation alone does not imply predictive power, so regression is applied when prediction is of interest. Example: moderate correlation r = 0.54 (p = 0.011) found between THE ranking and retraction rate; regression showed rank predicted 30.51% of variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal retraction policy standard (editor authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction policies should exist and clarify editor authority; among journals with retraction policies, many (observed 94% in cited analysis) allow editors to withdraw articles without authors' consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal-level policy presence and wording matter for how retractions are handled; editors are typically responsible for final decisions on retractions even if authors refuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of language and COPE membership as profiling variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Record whether the article and the retraction notice are published in English and whether the journal is a member of COPE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study most retracted articles were in English (96.67%) and most journals were COPE members (79.39%); these variables inform interpretation around visibility, standards, and reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic remedies and policy recommendations to reduce misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended interventions include: mandatory training in good research practices; improvements in the science reward system and stricter penalties; protection for whistleblowers; education in integrity and scientific ethics; improved training in logic, probability and statistics; establishment of uniform and transparent guidelines for retraction notices; changes in the peer review system; severe sanctions; and easing competitive pressure among scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are policy-level recommendations (cited from National Academy of Sciences and literature) intended to prevent misconduct and improve self-correction; they serve as criteria for evaluating institutional and national responses.
